title: David Fincher confirms AI use in Cliff Booth film
excerpt:
New information about the project has been announced.
Here is the confirmed news and its wider context.
body_md:
David Fincher has acknowledged using artificial intelligence in some capacity on The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, the Brad Pitt film written by Quentin Tarantino. The filmmaker discussed the subject during an appearance on The Big Picture podcast, adding a new development to the ongoing conversation about emerging technology in film production.

The headline accompanying the available report presents Fincher as receptive to the future of AI-assisted filmmaking. However, the excerpt does not specify the tools involved, the production stages in which they were employed or the extent of their contribution to the finished film. Those details are essential to any informed assessment of the decision.

The report also notes that some more contentious allegations surrounding the project remain unanswered and that Netflix had not responded to a request for clarification. Fincher's general acknowledgment should therefore not be treated as confirmation of every claim that has circulated about the production.

Cliff Booth is the character Pitt portrayed in Tarantino's 2019 film Once Upon a Time in Hollywood. Pitt won the Academy Award for supporting actor for that performance. The new project is notable for bringing together Tarantino's writing and Fincher's direction, two filmmakers with distinct creative approaches and substantial bodies of work.

Fincher has developed a reputation for meticulous control over visual presentation and close attention to technical detail. From an editorial perspective, his interest in exploring new tools can be considered within the wider history of digital filmmaking. That context does not establish the particular AI workflow used on this project.

The broader debate encompasses several different questions. Some applications may concern technical efficiency or production costs, while others raise issues involving creative authorship, consent, employment and the provenance of generated material. Evaluating these questions requires more information than a general statement that artificial intelligence was involved.

It is also important to distinguish between established digital techniques and newer generative systems rather than treating every computational production method as equivalent. The available excerpt does not provide enough technical information to make that distinction for the Cliff Booth film.

The confirmed development is that Fincher has acknowledged some AI use and expressed openness to the technology's future. The specific methods, their impact on artists and the scope of their contribution remain unresolved in the available material. Further clarification from the filmmakers or distributor would allow for a more substantive assessment of the production choices involved.
